name: Music Foundations
description: Sound organized in time: rhythm, pitch, notation, ensemble practice, and the listening vocabulary that turns hearing into perception.

observation.question: What must any account of music foundations explain?

creation.completionEvidence: Student produces an original artifact or proposal and defends its constraints

content.explanation: Sound organized in time: rhythm, pitch, notation, ensemble practice, and the listening vocabulary that turns hearing into perception. The branch organizes its concepts from first contact toward independent, integrated practice.
examples: Rhythm and Pulse: Clapping a 4/4 pulse while speaking a rhythm over it
Pitch and Melody: Singing a scale's gravity by resolving 7→1
Notation and Score Reading: Hearing a melody from its notation before playing it
Ensemble and Listening: Dropping volume to let a solo line through
nonExamples: Not rhythm and pulse: Counting aloud without an internal pulse
Not pitch and melody: Naming intervals without hearing them
Not notation and score reading: Reading note-by-note without phrase shape
Not ensemble and listening: Playing accurately but only at yourself

name: Rhythm and Pulse
description: Beat, meter, subdivision, and syncopation — the body-level grid that music moves against.

observation.question: Why does the body find the beat before the mind finds the notes?
observation.completionEvidence: Student can name the core elements of rhythm and pulse and say what each one does

principle.question: Why does rhythm and pulse work the way it does?
principle.completionEvidence: Student explains the mechanism in their own words, not by reciting the definition

integration.completionEvidence: Student links this concept to its prerequisites in one coherent account

creation.question: Design something original using rhythm and pulse.
creation.completionEvidence: Student produces an original artifact or proposal and defends its constraints

content.explanation: Rhythm is perceived in the body first: pulse predicts, meter groups, subdivision divides, syncopation delights by displacement. Steady pulse is a motor skill before it is a concept — the somatic line carries it. Reading rhythm notation is learning to see what the body already feels.
examples: Clapping a 4/4 pulse while speaking a rhythm over it
Hearing the backbeat shift in a familiar song
nonExamples: Counting aloud without an internal pulse
Treating notation as the rhythm rather than its map

name: Pitch and Melody
description: Intervals, scales, and melodic shape — how height and distance in pitch become tunes worth remembering.

content.explanation: Pitch relations come in families: intervals, ordered into scales that set a tonal gravity. Melody exploits that gravity — steps feel at home, leaps feel like journeys, resolution feels like arrival. Shape matters as much as content: contour is what listeners carry away.
examples: Singing a scale's gravity by resolving 7→1
Hearing a melody's contour in a new key as 'the same tune'
nonExamples: Melodies that wander because every note was chosen alone

description: The written map of sound: staff, clefs, note values, dynamics, and how a score encodes a performance.

content.explanation: Notation encodes pitch by height, time by shape, expression by markings — always lossily. Reading a score is reconstruction: decoding symbols back into imagined sound. The reader who audiates hears the page; the one who merely decodes names it.
examples: Hearing a melody from its notation before playing it
Marking breaths a score does not write

name: Ensemble and Listening
description: Making music with others: balance, blend, cueing, and the double listening to ensemble and self.

observation.question: What must you hear to play with others?
observation.completionEvidence: Student can name the core elements of ensemble and listening and say what each one does

principle.question: Why does ensemble and listening work the way it does?
principle.completionEvidence: Student explains the mechanism in their own words, not by reciting the definition

integration.completionEvidence: Student links this concept to its prerequisites in one coherent account

creation.question: Design something original using ensemble and listening.
creation.completionEvidence: Student produces an original artifact or proposal and defends its constraints

content.explanation: Ensemble playing splits attention: listen outward to the group's balance and inward to your own line, and keep both alive. Blend means adjusting timbre and volume to the whole; cueing means carrying intention visibly. It is the interpersonal line practiced through sound — a chamber group is a conversation with rules.
examples: Dropping volume to let a solo line through
nonExamples: Playing accurately but only at yourself
Loud sections drowning the line that carries the tune
